title: Voltage Divider Lab
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Clocks and Watches with AI
description: Adjust the input voltage and two resistors of a voltage divider, watch a bar-graph voltmeter show the output, and judge whether it is safe for a 3.3 V Pico pin.

educational.topic: Voltage dividers and safe input levels for the Pico
learningObjectives: Apply the voltage divider formula to calculate an output voltage.
Evaluate whether a divider output is safe for a 3.3 V Pico input pin.
Choose resistor values that bring a 5 V signal into the safe range with some margin.
prerequisites: Knowing that the Pico uses 3.3 V logic and its pins are not 5 V tolerant.

accessibility.notes: Screen-reader description provided; all controls are standard HTML elements.

controls.label: Input voltage Vin
controls.description: Voltage at the top of the divider.

controls.label: R1 (top)
controls.description: Resistor between Vin and the output point.

controls.label: R2 (bottom)
controls.description: Resistor between the output point and ground.

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Calculate, check, and judge against a safety limit
keyQuestions: Which resistor must be larger to bring 5 V down to about 3.3 V?
Why does the output stay the same when both resistors are multiplied by 10?
Is 3.33 V safe for a Pico pin? How could you add margin?
commonMisconceptions: Putting R1 and R2 in the formula the wrong way round.
Thinking the output depends on the size of the resistors rather than their ratio.
Thinking any voltage below 5 V is safe for a Pico pin.
assessmentOpportunities: Students correctly calculate Vout for any Vin, R1, and R2 shown in the MicroSim.
Students design a divider that turns 5 V into 3.0 to 3.3 V and justify their resistor choice.
Students explain why larger resistor values waste less current but give the same output ratio.
pedagogical.interactionPattern: Parameter exploration with live readout and verdict
